justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with a modest upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 56.8 is anchored heavily on the most recent observed value, assuming mean-reverting behavior and no major overnight catalysts. The slight upward drift to 57.1 at one week and 57.5 at one month reflects a gentle positive trend or fundamental bias I identified in the underlying data, perhaps driven by gradual momentum, improving conditions, or a slight structural tailwind. Each horizon incorporates diminishing weight on the most recent observation and greater weight on longer-run tendencies, which is why the estimates edge upward rather than holding flat.

The confidence interval widths expand significantly as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the compounding nature of forecast uncertainty. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 1.6 units is tight because short-term volatility is relatively constrained and there is little time for new information to substantially shift the outcome. By one week, the interval widens to roughly plus or minus 3.6 units, incorporating intra-week variability and the possibility of scheduled news or data releases. At one month, the interval spans 15 units, acknowledging that over four weeks a wide range of macroeconomic, behavioral, or situational factors can compound in either direction in ways that are fundamentally difficult to anticipate.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside even these wider intervals. On the upside, a sudden positive shock — such as a surprise policy announcement, stronger-than-expected data release, or a sentiment shift — could drive values well above 65 at the monthly horizon. On the downside, an adverse macro event, a liquidity disruption, or a sharp reversal in the prevailing trend could push values below 50. The one-day interval is most vulnerable to gap-risk events that occur outside of normal trading or observation hours, where the market or system in question has no ability to gradually adjust.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly normal or near-normal distributions of outcomes, which may understate tail risk. Real-world distributions often have fatter tails than a standard model implies, meaning extreme events are more likely than the stated 90% confidence interval suggests. Regime changes — where the underlying process fundamentally shifts — are the hardest risks to incorporate and represent the clearest pathway to outcomes that exceed my stated bounds at any horizon.
